name: 01 - First month free
ig_caption:
Most owners we speak to have already tried this themselves. They listed the place, got a few bookings, then spent a season answering messages at 1am and wondering whether the rate was right.

So we made the first month easy to say yes to. No management fee for month one. No setup fee. No lock-in — leave whenever you want.

We work on commission. If your place doesn't earn, we don't earn. That's the whole arrangement, and it's the reason we're picky about which homes we take on.

Send us the address and we'll come back with what we think it would do.
fb_caption:
A straight offer for second-home owners in Mumbai and Goa: your first month with us is free.

No management fee for month one, no setup fee, and no long-term contract. We work purely on commission — if the property doesn't earn, we don't earn either.

What that month covers: listing rebuilt and photographed properly, pricing set and actively managed, guest messages handled end to end, housekeeping and turnovers coordinated, and a monthly statement you can actually read.

Most owners we meet aren't short of interest in their property. They're short of the time it takes to run it well — and that gap is usually what costs them, not the market.

Send us the address and we'll tell you what we think it would earn. No obligation.

name: 02 - 83 percent occupancy
ig_caption:
A one-bedroom in Juhu. Not a villa, not a view — a well-run flat in a good location.

83% occupancy over the last twelve months. 4.88 stars across 104 reviews. Four years of hosting behind it.

Nothing clever going on. The listing is honest, the photos match the flat, the price moves with demand instead of sitting still, and guests get an answer in minutes rather than hours.

83% isn't 100%, and we won't pretend otherwise — the empty nights are mostly deliberate, because dropping the rate far enough to fill every one costs more than it earns.

Your place doesn't need to be a landmark to run like this. It needs someone paying attention to it every week.

Book a free 15-minute discovery call and we'll tell you what your place would earn.
fb_caption:
Real numbers from a property we manage in Juhu, Mumbai: 83% occupancy across the last 365 days, a 4.88 star rating, and 104 reviews over four years of hosting. Figures as of 25 August.

It's a one-bedroom flat. No pool, no sea view. What it has is a listing that tells the truth, photographs that match what guests walk into, a nightly rate that moves with demand, and replies that go out in minutes.

We're sharing it because owners tend to assume the ceiling is set by the property. Location and condition matter, obviously — but the gap between an averagely run listing and a well-run one is usually larger than the gap between two properties.

And to be straight about the number: 83% is a good result, not a perfect one. Chasing the last 17% usually means cutting the rate below what the nights are worth. We'd rather leave a few gaps than run the place cheap.

Past performance on one home isn't a promise about yours. Book a free 15-minute discovery call and we'll give you a realistic range for your property — not a sales number.

name: 03 - Stop guessing your rate
ig_caption:
Here's where most self-managed listings lose money: the price never moves.

One rate for weekdays, one for weekends, maybe a bump for New Year. Meanwhile a long weekend gets announced, flights into Goa fill up, and the villa down the road quietly goes up 40% — while your calendar sells out three weeks early at last year's price.

Selling out early isn't a win. It usually means you were cheap.

We reprice every week: demand, events, flight loads, what comparable homes nearby are actually charging. Sometimes that means going up. Sometimes it means dropping to fill a soft Tuesday. Both are decisions, not defaults.

DM 'NUMBERS' and we'll send you the breakdown for your area.
fb_caption:
A question worth asking yourself: when did you last change your nightly rate?

If the answer is "at the start of the season", you're almost certainly leaving money on the table — and the tell is a calendar that fills up too early. A booked-out December looks like success. Often it just means the price was low enough that everyone said yes.

Pricing a short-let well means watching things that change weekly: long weekends and festival dates, flight loads into Goa and Mumbai, what genuinely comparable homes nearby are charging right now, and how far ahead your own bookings are coming in.

We do that review every week for every property we manage. Some weeks the rate goes up. Some weeks we drop it to fill a quiet midweek gap, because an empty night earns nothing.

Message us the word NUMBERS and we'll send you a breakdown of what rates are doing in your area this season.

name: 04 - You run the home
ig_caption:
The most common thing we hear: "I don't want to hand over my house."

You're not handing it over. You decide who stays, which dates you keep for yourself, and what the house rules are. You keep the keys.

What we take on is the work: the listing, the pricing, guest messages at every hour, housekeeping and turnovers, maintenance when something breaks, and a monthly statement that shows where the money went.

Owner keeps the home. Co-host runs the operation. That's the split.

See how it works — link in bio.
fb_caption:
"I don't want to lose control of my own house" is the objection we hear most, and it's a fair one. So here's the actual division of labour.

You keep: the keys, the final say on your own booking dates, the house rules, the standard the property is held to, and the right to walk away whenever you want.

We take: building and maintaining the listing, setting and revising the nightly rate, every guest message from enquiry to check-out, housekeeping and turnovers between stays, calling the electrician when something fails, and sending you a statement each month that explains what came in and what went out.

We operate as a co-host on your listing. Nothing is transferred, nothing is locked in.

If you've been putting this off because handing over the house felt like a big step — it isn't one. Message us and we'll walk you through exactly what changes and what doesn't.

name: 06 - AC died at 11.40pm
ig_caption:
11:40pm. AC packs up in a full house.

11:41pm — guest messages. Answered in under four minutes, fan and extra bedding sorted for the night. 12:20am — technician booked for first thing. 8:15am — fixed. The owner found out over coffee, in a message that started with "handled".

Nobody leaves a five-star review for an AC that worked. They absolutely leave a one-star for an AC that didn't and a host who was asleep.

This is the part of co-hosting nobody advertises, and it's most of the job.

That's what a co-host is for.
fb_caption:
A normal night on the operations side.

11:40pm, the air conditioning fails in an occupied flat. The guest messages and gets a reply in under four minutes — a fan and extra bedding go up, so nobody spends the night awake and angry. By 12:20am a technician is booked for the morning. By 8:15am it's repaired.

The owner heard about it once, over coffee, in a message that opened with "handled".

We're posting this because the marketing version of this business is photographs of nice bedrooms, and the real version is what happens when something breaks at midnight. Guests don't rate you on the AC working. They rate you on what happened when it stopped.

If your property is currently covered by you personally answering your phone at midnight, that's the thing worth outsourcing first.

name: 05 - Your home, your account
ig_caption:
We work as a co-host on your Airbnb account. Not our listing with your house in it — your listing, your account, your name on it.

That matters more than it sounds. The reviews build under your profile. The booking history stays yours. If you ever want to run it yourself again, or move to someone else, you take all of it with you and nothing has to be rebuilt.

Full access on your side. No handover. No exit penalty.

We'd rather you stay because the numbers are good than because leaving is a hassle.

Ask us anything — DMs are open.
fb_caption:
Something worth checking before you sign with any management company: whose account is the listing on?

We work as a co-host on yours. You stay the owner of record. The listing, the reviews, the booking history and the guest relationship all sit under your profile — not ours.

The reason we're specific about it: reviews are the single hardest asset to rebuild in this business. If a management company runs your property under their own account and you later part ways, you don't take years of five-star reviews with you. You start over. That's a genuine cost, and it's one a lot of owners only discover on the way out.

You get full access throughout. There's no handover, no lock-in, and no penalty for leaving.

Ask us anything — we'd rather answer the awkward questions upfront.

name: 07 - Guest reviews
ig_caption:
Three homes we co-host. Three sets of guests. Three five-star stays.

None of these reviews are about us. They're about Mandakini finding the house spotless, Bernard finding it exactly as described, Jigna having a month where the communication simply worked.

That's the point. The owner's name is on the listing, the reviews build on their profile, and our job is making sure the standard holds every single time — the turnovers, the replies, the small things guests notice and mention.

Good reviews aren't luck. They're a handful of unglamorous things done properly, on repeat.

Book a free 15-minute discovery call and we'll talk about your place.
fb_caption:
Three homes we co-host in Goa and Mumbai. Three recent five-star reviews, copied verbatim from Airbnb.

Worth being clear about whose reviews these are: they belong to the owners. The listings are in their names, the ratings build on their profiles, and if they ever stopped working with us they would take every one of these with them. That is deliberate — we co-host, we don't take over.

What we're responsible for is the part guests end up writing about. The house being spotless on arrival. The description matching what they walk into. A reply arriving in minutes rather than the next morning. None of it is clever. It's just done, every time, without the owner having to think about it.

That's what a co-host is for, and it's why owners who were doing this themselves tend to say the reviews got better, not just the calendar.
